expected.claim: Fix an initial pair $(s,x_0)$ and a closed ball $K=\overline B(x_0,r)$. On a sufficiently short one-sided interval $J$ adjoining $s$, absolute continuity of the integrals of $m_K,L_K$ gives $\int_Jm_K\le r$ and $\int_JL_K<1$. On continuous curves taking values in $K$, define $\Phi(X)(t)=x_0+\int_s^t b(q,X(q))dq,$ with the oriented integral when J lies to the left of s. The integrand is measurable because $q\mapsto(q,X(q))$ is continuous and b is Borel; it is integrable because $|b(q,X(q))|\le m_K(q)$ almost everywhere. The map preserves the closed sup-norm ball of radius r about the constant curve $x_0$, and $\|\Phi(X)-\Phi(Y)\|_\infty\le(\int_JL_K)\|X-Y\|_\infty$. By [F1] it has a unique fixed point. The integral FTC [F2] makes this curve absolutely continuous and a solution almost everywhere.

If two solutions have the same value at one time and remain in a compact K on a common compact interval, partition that interval into finitely many subintervals on which $\int L_K<1$. On each subinterval beginning at a time where the solutions agree, their integral equations bound their sup-norm difference by $(\int L_K)$ times itself, so the difference is zero. Induction over the partition proves uniqueness throughout the common interval. Their union therefore defines a unique maximal solution. If a maximal endpoint $\tau$ lies in $(0,T)$ and the path stays in a compact K as $t\to\tau$, then $|\dot X(t)|\le m_K(t)$ makes $X(t)$ Cauchy at $\tau$. Its limit is finite, and step 1.1 restarted at that limit extends the solution, contradicting maximality. Hence an interior maximal endpoint forces the path to leave every compact set.

Assume the spatial derivative hypothesis. On a short interval and compact ball as in step 1.1, solutions from nearby initial points remain in a common compact ball. The contraction estimate gives $\|X(\cdot;s,x_0+h)-X(\cdot;s,x_0)\|_\infty\le C|h|$. Write $\Delta_h(t)=X(t;s,x_0+h)-X(t;s,x_0)$. The state-variable fundamental theorem of calculus [F3] gives $\Delta_h(t)=h+\int_s^t A_h(q)\Delta_h(q)dq,\quad A_h(q)=\int_0^1D_xb(q,X(q;s,x_0)+\theta\Delta_h(q))d\theta.$ The matrix equation $V(t)=I_d+\int_s^tA(q)V(q)dq$ has a unique continuous solution by the contraction argument of step 1.1, since $\int_JL_K<1$. Subtracting its product with h from the equation for $\Delta_h$ gives $\Delta_h(t)-V(t)h=\int_s^t A_h(q)(\Delta_h(q)-V(q)h)dq+\int_s^t(A_h(q)-A(q))V(q)h\,dq.$ Taking sup norms and absorbing the first term bounds the left side by $C|h|\int_J\|A_h-A\|dq=o(|h|)$. Repeating on a finite cover by overlapping short intervals gives $C^1$ dependence throughout each common flow domain and continuous dependence in the uniform path norm on trajectories existing through the full interval.

Uniqueness makes the time map from s to t injective. Continuous dependence makes its domain open; solving backward from time t shows its image is open and its inverse is the backward flow, which is $C^1$ by step 3.1. The chain rule [F5] says the derivative of the inverse times V is the identity. Thus the time map is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism between its open domain and image.

Fix a compact flow tube and a compact set K of states it visits. Choose a countable dense subset Q of K. By [F6], outside one null set the functions $m_K,L_K$ and $s\mapsto b(s,q)$ for all $q\in Q$ have their values as limits of local averages. At such times, the average of $b(s,x)$ over a shrinking interval converges to $b(s,x)$ uniformly for $x\in K$: approximate x by q\in Q, bound the average error by $|x-q|$ times the average of L_K, and use continuity/Lipschitz continuity of the time slice at s; then let q approach x. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T>0$, $d\ge1$, and let $(\mu_t,v_t)$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$, with space-time law $M(dt,dx)=dt\,\mu_t(dx)$. For $\varepsilon>0$, let $\rho_\varepsilon$ be the strictly positive centered Gaussian probability density with covariance $\varepsilon I_d$, and define
$$p_t^\varepsilon(x)=\int\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)d\mu_t(y),\quad j_t^\varepsilon(x)=\int\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)v_t(y)d\mu_t(y),\quad v_t^\varepsilon(x)=j_t^\varepsilon(x)/p_t^\varepsilon(x).$$
Then $p_t^\varepsilon$ is a strictly positive smooth probability density for each $t$, $t\mapsto\mu_t^\varepsilon$ is narrowly continuous, $v_t^\varepsilon$ is Borel and locally Lipschitz in $x$ with local magnitude and Lipschitz bounds integrable in time, and $(\mu_t*\rho_\varepsilon,v_t^\varepsilon)$ solves the continuity equation. For almost every $t$,
$$\int|v_t^\varepsilon(x)|^2p_t^\varepsilon(x)dx\le\int|v_t(y)|^2d\mu_t(y).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T>0$, let $d\ge1$, and let $b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be Borel. Suppose that for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ there are nonnegative $m_K,L_K\in L^1(0,T)$ such that for almost every $t$, $|b(t,x)|\le m_K(t)$ and $|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|\le L_K(t)|x-y|$ for all $x,y\in K$. For each $(s,x_0)$ there is a unique maximal absolutely continuous solution $X(\cdot;s,x_0)$ of $\dot X=b(t,X)$ with $X(s)=x_0$, where maximal means that it has no solution extension to a strictly larger interval in $[0,T]$; any maximal endpoint lying in $(0,T)$ can occur only if the trajectory leaves every compact subset of $\mathbb R^d$. If, in addition, $b(t,\cdot)$ is continuously differentiable for almost every $t$ and $D_xb$ has integrable local bounds, then the set of initial points whose trajectories exist between any fixed pair of times is open, its time map is one-to-one onto an open image with both map and inverse continuously differentiable, and the path map into the uniform path space is continuous on the set of trajectories existing through the full interval. On compact flow tubes the dependence on the starting time is locally absolutely continuous and satisfies $\partial_sX(t;s,x)=-D_xX(t;s,x)b(s,x)$ for almost every s, simultaneously for x in the tube. The spatial derivative $V_t=D_{x_0}X(t;s,x_0)$ satisfies $\dot V_t=D_xb(t,X_t)V_t$, $V_s=I_d$, almost everywhere.

Assume countable choice. If $P$ is Polish and $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure on $P$, then for every Borel $A\subseteq P$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

Assume Countable Choice. For every integer $d\ge1$ there is a nonnegative function $\rho_d:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with continuous partial derivatives of every order, support exactly $[-1,1]^d$, strictly positive on $(-1,1)^d$, and Lebesgue integral $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_d(x)\,dx=1$. Here the support is the closure of the set where the function is nonzero.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Then $a$ is measurable, $N$ is Borel and Lebesgue-null, and the Borel representative $\bar v(t,x)=0$ for $t\in N$ and $\bar v(t,x)=v(t,x)$ for $t\notin N$ agrees with $v$ $M$-almost everywhere. $$p_t^\varepsilon(x)=\int\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)d\mu_t(y),\quad j_t^\varepsilon(x)=\int\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)\bar v_t(y)d\mu_t(y),\quad v_t^\varepsilon(x)=j_t^\varepsilon(x)/p_t^\varepsilon(x).$$
Then $p_t^\varepsilon$ is a strictly positive smooth probability density for each $t$, $t\mapsto\mu_t^\varepsilon$ is narrowly continuous, $v_t^\varepsilon$ is Borel and locally Lipschitz in $x$ with local magnitude and Lipschitz bounds integrable in time, and $(\mu_t*\rho_\varepsilon,v_t^\varepsilon)$ solves the continuity equation. For almost every $t$,
$$\int|v_t^\varepsilon(x)|^2p_t^\varepsilon(x)dx\le\int|v_t(y)|^2d\mu_t(y).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T>0$, let $d\ge1$, and let $b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be Borel. Suppose that for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ there are nonnegative $m_K,L_K\in L^1(0,T)$ such that for almost every $t$, $|b(t,x)|\le m_K(t)$ and $|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|\le L_K(t)|x-y|$ for all $x,y\in K$. For each $(s,x_0)$ there is a unique maximal absolutely continuous solution $X(\cdot;s,x_0)$ of $\dot X=b(t,X)$ with $X(s)=x_0$, where maximal means that it has no solution extension to a strictly larger interval in $[0,T]$; any maximal endpoint lying in $(0,T)$ can occur only if the trajectory leaves every compact subset of $\mathbb R^d$. If, in addition, $b(t,\cdot)$ is continuously differentiable for almost every $t$ and $D_xb$ has integrable local bounds, then the set of initial points whose trajectories exist between any fixed pair of times is open, its time map is one-to-one onto an open image with both map and inverse continuously differentiable, and the path map into the uniform path space is continuous on the set of trajectories existing through the full interval. On compact flow tubes the dependence on the starting time is locally absolutely continuous and satisfies $\partial_sX(t;s,x)=-D_xX(t;s,x)b(s,x)$ for almost every s, simultaneously for x in the tube. The spatial derivative $V_t=D_{x_0}X(t;s,x_0)$ satisfies $\dot V_t=D_xb(t,X_t)V_t$, $V_s=I_d$, almost everywhere.

Assume countable choice. If $P$ is Polish and $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure on $P$, then for every Borel $A\subseteq P$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

Assume Countable Choice. For every integer $d\ge1$ there is a nonnegative function $\rho_d:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with continuous partial derivatives of every order, support exactly $[-1,1]^d$, strictly positive on $(-1,1)^d$, and Lebesgue integral $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_d(x)\,dx=1$. Here the support is the closure of the set where the function is nonzero.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume countable choice. If $P$ is Polish and $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure on $P$, then for every Borel $A\subseteq P$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

expected.claim: Apply [F2] to $v^\varepsilon$ and denote by $D_t$ the open set of initial points whose trajectories exist from time 0 through t, and by $E_t=X_t^\varepsilon(D_t)$ its open image. Fix $t\in(0,T]$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(E_t)$. For $0\le r\le t$ and $x\in D_{r,t}$, the set of states whose trajectories exist from r to t, define $\psi(r,x)=f(X^\varepsilon(t;r,x))$; extend it by zero outside $D_{r,t}$. Since $\operatorname{supp}f$ is compactly contained in $E_t$, its backward images form a compact subset of the flow domain. Thus $\psi$ has compact spatial support uniformly in r, is continuously differentiable in x, and is absolutely continuous in r locally. The start-time derivative from [F2] and the flow identity give $\partial_r\psi=\nabla f(X(t;r,x))\cdot[-D_xX(t;r,x)v_r^\varepsilon(x)]=-v_r^\varepsilon(x)\cdot\nabla_x\psi$ almost everywhere.

The weak continuity-equation identity extends from smooth compact tests to compactly supported tests that are $C^1$ in x and absolutely continuous in r with locally integrable time derivative: multiply by a time cutoff, convolve in time and space on a fixed compact neighborhood, and pass to the limit. The terms converge because $p^\varepsilon$ is locally bounded, $p^\varepsilon v^\varepsilon$ is locally integrable in time and space by finite action, and the test and its spatial gradient converge uniformly while its time derivative converges in $L^1$. Apply this extension to $\eta(r)\psi(r,x)$ from step 1.1 for every smooth compactly supported time cutoff $\eta$. The transport equation leaves $\int\eta'(r)F(r)dr=0$, so $F(r)=\int\psi(r,x)d\mu_r^\varepsilon(x)$ is constant on (0,t). Continuity of the flow and of $\mu_r^\varepsilon$ extends the identity to r=0,t, so $\int f(y)d\mu_t^\varepsilon(y)=\int_{D_t}f(X_t^\varepsilon(x))d\mu_0^\varepsilon(x).$ Uniform mollification extends this equality to every $f\in C_c(E_t)$; since both measures are finite, the uniform limit passes through their integrals. Inner regularity [F3] then identifies the finite Borel measures on $E_t$: $\mu_t^\varepsilon|_{E_t}=(X_t^\varepsilon)_\#(\mu_0^\varepsilon|_{D_t}).$

Let $\tau(x)$ be the maximal forward existence time. The measure identity of step 2.1, first for bounded nonnegative truncations of $|v_t^\varepsilon|^2$ and then by monotone convergence, gives $\int\!\int_0^{\min\{T,\tau(x)\}}|v_r^\varepsilon(X_r^\varepsilon(x))|^2dr\,d\mu_0^\varepsilon(x)\le\int_0^T\!\int|v_r^\varepsilon(y)|^2d\mu_r^\varepsilon(y)dr<\infty.$ Tonelli [F4] shows that for $\mu_0^\varepsilon$-almost every x the path has finite squared speed integral up to its maximal endpoint. Holder then makes its total path length finite. Such a path is Cauchy at any finite endpoint; it cannot escape every compact set, contradicting [F2] if an endpoint lies in $(0,T)$. At T it has a finite limit and extends continuously to T. Thus $\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_T)=1$.

For each t, step 2.1 identifies $\mu_t^\varepsilon$ on $E_t$ with the pushforward of $\mu_0^\varepsilon|_{D_t}$. Since $D_t\supseteq D_T$ has full $\mu_0^\varepsilon$-measure by step 3.1, this pushforward is a probability supported on $E_t$. Therefore $\mu_t^\varepsilon(E_t)=1$, and the restricted-measure identity is equality on all of $\mathbb R^d$. This proves $\mu_t^\varepsilon=(X_t^\varepsilon)_\#\mu_0^\varepsilon$ for every t, with the unique flow given by [F2].

For this fixed t define the restricted finite pushforward $
u_t$ on $E_t$ by $
u_t(B)=\mu_0^\varepsilon(\{x\in D_t:X_t^\varepsilon(x)\in B\})$ for Borel $B\subseteq E_t$. The set is Borel because $X_t^\varepsilon$ is continuous on the open domain $D_t$; preimages preserve disjoint unions, so $

u_t=\mu_t^\varepsilon|_{E_t}$.

Let $\mathscr D=\{(r,x):x\in D_r\}$. This domain is relatively open in $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$ and $(r,x)\mapsto X_r^\varepsilon(x)$ is continuous on it: cover any compact trajectory segment through $(r,x)$ by finitely many local flow neighborhoods from [F2] and patch their continuous dependence on the initial point; time continuity follows from the integral equation. Thus the integrand is Borel; extend it by zero off $\mathscr D$. For each t, step 2.1 identifies $\mu_t^\varepsilon|_{E_t}$ with $
u_t=(X_t^\varepsilon)_\#(\mu_0^\varepsilon|_{D_t})$, where this restricted pushforward is the finite measure defined in step 2.1. Since $D_T\subseteq D_t$ and $\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_T)=1$ by step 3.1, $
u_t(E_t)=\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_t)=1$. Hence $\mu_t^\varepsilon(E_t)=1$, and the equality of restricted measures extends to all Borel subsets of $\mathbb R^d$. expected.quote: Let S be Polish in the sense of [[def-polish-space]]. A **Borel probability law on S** is a countably additive measure on $\mathcal B(S)$ with total mass one. Here $\mathcal B(S)$ is [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]] and probability measure means [[def-probability-measure]]. A compatible complete metric may be fixed for a construction; it is not additional data in the law. The empty space admits no such law, since its measure must be both zero and one.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $X,Y$ be second-countable topological spaces and give $X\times Y$ the
product topology. Then
$$\mathcal B(X\times Y)=\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(Y).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. If
$E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, then $E_x \in \mathcal B$ for every
$x \in X$ and $E^y \in \mathcal A$ for every $y \in Y$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
[[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]].

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple ([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]).

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is

> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $T>0$ and let $t\mapsto\mu_t$ be a narrowly continuous curve of Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R^d$, where narrow continuity means convergence against every bounded continuous real test function. For a product-Borel set $E\subseteq[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$, write $E_t=\{x:(t,x)\in E\}$ and define $M(E)=\int_0^T\mu_t(E_t)dt$. Then $t\mapsto\mu_t$ is a probability kernel, $M$ is a finite Borel measure of total mass $T$, and for every nonnegative product-Borel $f$, $\int f\,dM=\int_0^T\int f(t,x)d\mu_t(x)dt$.

Assume AC. Let $T>0$ and let $(\mu_t,v_t)$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$. Then $t\mapsto\mu_t$ belongs to $AC^2([0,T];\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d))$ and, for almost every $t$,
$$|\dot\mu_t|\le\left(\int|v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)\right)^{1/2}.$$

Assume AC. Let $T>0$ and let $(\mu_t,v_t)$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$. There is a Borel probability law $\eta$ on $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ such that $(e_t)_\#\eta=\mu_t$ for every $t$, and for $\eta$-almost every path $\gamma$, $\gamma$ is absolutely continuous, $\gamma(0)$ has law $\mu_0$, and $\dot\gamma(t)=v_t(\gamma(t))$ for almost every $t$. Its expected path action equals the Eulerian action:
$$\int\!\int_0^T|\dot\gamma(t)|^2dt\,d\eta(\gamma)=\int_0^T\!\int|v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)dt.$$

Let $(X,\mu)$ and $(Y,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces, let
$1 \le p < \infty$, and let $F : X \times Y \to \mathbb{C}$ be measurable with

$$ \int_Y \|F(\cdot,y)\|_{L^p(X)}\,d\nu(y) < \infty. $$

Then the function
$$ H(x) := \int_Y |F(x,y)|\,d\nu(y) $$
belongs to $L^p(X)$ and

$$ \|H\|_{L^p(X)} \le \int_Y \|F(\cdot,y)\|_{L^p(X)}\,d\nu(y). $$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $T>0$ and $\mu\in AC^2([0,T];\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d))$, then the metric derivative
$$|\dot\mu_t|=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{W_2(\mu_{t+h},\mu_t)}{|h|}$$
exists for almost every $t\in(0,T)$, is measurable and belongs to $L^2(0,T)$. For all $0\le s\le t\le T$,
$$W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)\le\int_s^t|\dot\mu_r|dr.$$
It is the least nonnegative square-integrable upper control: if $g\in L^2(0,T)$ and $W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)\le\int_s^t g(r)dr$ for all $s\le t$, then $|\dot\mu_t|\le g(t)$ almost everywhere.

Let S be Polish in the sense of [[def-polish-space]]. A **Borel probability law on S** is a countably additive measure on $\mathcal B(S)$ with total mass one. Here $\mathcal B(S)$ is [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]] and probability measure means [[def-probability-measure]]. A compatible complete metric may be fixed for a construction; it is not additional data in the law. The empty space admits no such law, since its measure must be both zero and one.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

expected.claim: For $0\le s<t\le T$, push $\eta$ forward by $\gamma\mapsto(\gamma(s),\gamma(t))$ to obtain a coupling of $\mu_s,\mu_t$ by [F1]. For almost every path, absolute continuity gives $|\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)|\le\int_s^t|\dot\gamma(r)|dr$. Minkowski [F2], applied with the path probability space and Lebesgue measure on $[s,t]$, yields $W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)\le\left(\int\left(\int_s^t|\dot\gamma(r)|dr\right)^2d\eta\right)^{1/2}\le\int_s^t\left(\int|\dot\gamma(r)|^2d\eta\right)^{1/2}dr.$ The marginal identity and the pathwise velocity identity in [F1] identify the inner integral for almost every r as $\int|v_r(x)|^2d\mu_r(x)$. By [F3], the metric derivative exists almost everywhere and is no larger than any nonnegative $L^2$ upper control. Applying it to $g$ from step 1.1 gives $|\dot\mu_t|\le g(t)$ almost everywhere, as claimed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T>0$, $d\ge1$, and let $(\mu_t,v_t)$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$, with space-time law $M(dt,dx)=dt\,\mu_t(dx)$. For $\varepsilon>0$, let $\rho_\varepsilon$ be the strictly positive centered Gaussian probability density with covariance $\varepsilon I_d$, and define
$$p_t^\varepsilon(x)=\int\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)d\mu_t(y),\quad j_t^\varepsilon(x)=\int\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)v_t(y)d\mu_t(y),\quad v_t^\varepsilon(x)=j_t^\varepsilon(x)/p_t^\varepsilon(x).$$
Then $p_t^\varepsilon$ is a strictly positive smooth probability density for each $t$, $t\mapsto\mu_t^\varepsilon$ is narrowly continuous, $v_t^\varepsilon$ is Borel and locally Lipschitz in $x$ with local magnitude and Lipschitz bounds integrable in time, and $(\mu_t*\rho_\varepsilon,v_t^\varepsilon)$ solves the continuity equation. For almost every $t$,
$$\int|v_t^\varepsilon(x)|^2p_t^\varepsilon(x)dx\le\int|v_t(y)|^2d\mu_t(y).$$

Assume AC. Let $(\mu_t^\varepsilon,v_t^\varepsilon)$ be the Gaussian-regularized solution from the preceding lemma on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$, and write $\mu_t^\varepsilon=p_t^\varepsilon(x)dx$. There is a unique maximal local flow $X_t^\varepsilon(x)$ solving $\dot X_t^\varepsilon(x)=v_t^\varepsilon(X_t^\varepsilon(x))$, $X_0^\varepsilon(x)=x$. For $\mu_0^\varepsilon$-almost every x the path exists on all of $[0,T]$, the map from x to its path is Borel on this full-measure domain, and for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\mu_t^\varepsilon=(X_t^\varepsilon)_\#\mu_0^\varepsilon.$$
Assume AC. A family $\mathcal A$ of Borel probabilities on a Polish space S is tight if and only if it is relatively sequentially compact for weak convergence.

A family $\mathcal A$ of Borel probabilities on a metric space S is **tight** if, for every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a compact $K\subseteq S$ such that $\mu(S\setminus K)<\varepsilon$ for every $\mu\in\mathcal A$. One K must work for the whole family. Compactness is [[def-metric-compactness]]. The empty family is tight, witnessed by the empty compact set.
Assume AC. If $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ on a Polish space, then $\{\mu,\mu_1,\mu_2,\ldots\}$ is tight.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $T>0$ and give $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ the uniform topology. Define
$$\mathcal E(\gamma)=\begin{cases}\int_0^T|\dot\gamma(t)|^2dt,&\gamma\text{ is absolutely continuous with }\dot\gamma\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^d),\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
Then $\mathcal E$ is lower semicontinuous. More precisely,
$$\mathcal E(\gamma)=\sup_{0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T}\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\frac{|\gamma(t_{i+1})-\gamma(t_i)|^2}{t_{i+1}-t_i},$$
where the supremum is over all finite partitions of $[0,T]$.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Assume Dependent Choice. Let $M$ be a finite Radon Borel measure on $\mathbb R^n$, where $n\ge1$. Then $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ is dense in $L^2(M)$.

Assume countable choice. If $P$ is Polish and $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure on $P$, then for every Borel $A\subseteq P$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

For this page, a Borel measure $\mu$ on a locally compact Hausdorff space is
**Radon** when $\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact $K$, and, for every Borel
$E$ and every open $U$,
$$\mu(E)=\inf_{E\subseteq V\text{ open}}\mu(V),\qquad \mu(U)=\sup_{K\subseteq U\text{ compact}}\mu(K).$$
Cohn calls this convention regular. It does not assert compact inner
approximation for arbitrary Borel $E$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X,\mu)$ and $(Y,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces, let
$1 \le p < \infty$, and let $F : X \times Y \to \mathbb{C}$ be measurable with

$$ \int_Y \|F(\cdot,y)\|_{L^p(X)}\,d\nu(y) < \infty. $$

Then the function
$$ H(x) := \int_Y |F(x,y)|\,d\nu(y) $$
belongs to $L^p(X)$ and

$$ \|H\|_{L^p(X)} \le \int_Y \|F(\cdot,y)\|_{L^p(X)}\,d\nu(y). $$

Let S be Polish in the sense of [[def-polish-space]]. A **Borel probability law on S** is a countably additive measure on $\mathcal B(S)$ with total mass one. Here $\mathcal B(S)$ is [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]] and probability measure means [[def-probability-measure]]. A compatible complete metric may be fixed for a construction; it is not additional data in the law. The empty space admits no such law, since its measure must be both zero and one.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let

$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on

   rectangle formula.
